opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the more interesting open questions right now, and I'm a bit skeptical of the strong version of it.

The appeal is obvious. Code and math are domains where you can actually check the answer. You run the unit tests, you verify the proof, and you get a clean reward signal. So reinforcement learning works really well there, and we've seen huge gains. The hope is that the model is learning something like general "reasoning" along the way, and that this transfers to everything else: writing, strategy, advice, whatever.

I think there's some transfer. When you train a model to break a problem into steps, backtrack when something doesn't work, and check its own work, those habits do show up in other places. You can see it in the reasoning traces. The model picks up these little cognitive strategies, like "wait, let me reconsider," that look fairly domain-general.

But I don't think it's free, and I don't think it's automatic. A lot of what makes a model good in fuzzy domains is taste and judgment: knowing what a good essay is, what a good piece of advice is, what a human actually wants. There's no unit test for that. And if you lean really hard on verifiable rewards, you can get these slightly jagged models that are superhuman at some competition math problem and then make a really dumb mistake on something a kid would get right. The intelligence isn't as uniform as we'd like to imagine.

So the way I'd put it is that verifiable domains are where the low-hanging fruit is for RL, so that's where progress is fastest, and some of it bleeds over. But I'd be careful about assuming that getting really good at code means you've solved everything else. For the non-verifiable stuff, we still need better ways of generating signal, whether that's better reward models, LLM judges that don't just get gamed, or something we haven't figured out yet. To me that's one of the big unsolved problems.

r001.rationale: The response says transfer from verifiable tasks is partial and cautions that success at code does not mean everything else is solved.

r002.rationale: It discusses reinforcement learning and verifiable rewards, but does not identify laboratories’ training data choices as a source of selective optimization.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there's something real there, but I'd be careful about how far the transfer goes. Code is a pretty special domain. It's the one place where we have a nearly perfect verifier: you write the program, you run the tests, and you get a crisp signal back. Math is similar in some ways. So when you do reinforcement learning on these tasks, you get this very clean reward, and the models climb that gradient really fast. That's why the progress in coding has been so dramatic relative to a lot of other things.

The question is what you actually get for free when you do that. I think you do get some generalization. Writing good code requires you to hold a problem in your head, decompose it, notice when something is inconsistent, backtrack. Those are fairly general cognitive skills, and I think they do leak into other domains to some extent. The models get a bit more careful, a bit more structured in their reasoning. That's real.

But I'm skeptical of the strong version of the claim, which is that if you just push hard enough on verifiable tasks, everything else comes along for the ride. A lot of what people actually care about isn't verifiable in that sense. Writing a good essay, giving good advice, making a judgment call where the information is incomplete, understanding what a person actually wants versus what they said. There's no unit test for that. And when you look at the models today, you see exactly this gap. They're incredible at the stuff where you can check the answer, and they're kind of meh, honestly, at a lot of the stuff where you can't. They'll write a working function in seconds and then produce a document that's bland and slightly off in ways that are hard to pin down.

So I think of it as a spiky profile. The spikes are wherever we have a verifier, and the valleys are wherever we don't. Getting better at code makes the spikes taller, and it raises the floor a little, but it doesn't flatten the whole thing. To really get the rest of it you need something else, probably some way of learning from much messier, noisier feedback, more like how people learn from experience. We don't really have that yet. So I'd say coding is the leading indicator of where the models are going, but it's not a proxy for everything.

r001.rationale: The response says gains on verifiable tasks raise some general skills but do not make everything else improve equally, describing a spiky profile rather than broad transfer.

r002.rationale: It discusses reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks and their effects, but does not identify laboratories’ training-data choices as a source of selective optimization.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a hypothesis, and I’m not sure how far it goes. If you train a model to be really good at code, you’re teaching it a lot of things that seem broadly useful: breaking down problems, keeping track of constraints, checking whether an approach worked, and trying something else. So I would expect some transfer.

But there’s a distinction between getting better at those operations and getting better at everything we care about. With code, you can run it. You have this external signal that tells you whether you’re making progress. If you’re giving someone advice, or writing something insightful, what’s the equivalent of passing the unit tests? The feedback is much harder to specify.

So the question for me is how much of intelligence is a shared capability that you can improve in one domain and then apply elsewhere, versus how much requires experience and feedback in that particular domain. I don’t think we should assume the transfer is automatic. It’s an empirical question. You’d want to see the model getting better in places where you didn’t directly train it to get better.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes improvement on verifiable tasks from improvement in everything people care about and says transfer should not be assumed automatic.

r002.rationale: It discusses domain-specific experience and feedback, but does not identify laboratories’ choices of training data as selectively optimizing model abilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s something to it, but I wouldn’t take it for granted. Code is a particularly nice environment because you can try something, execute it, and get feedback. You can train on whether the thing actually worked, instead of whether it looked like a good answer to someone.

The interesting question is what the model learns in the process. Does it learn a bunch of tricks that are specific to programming, or does it learn more general strategies—breaking a problem down, checking assumptions, noticing when it’s going down the wrong path? If it’s learning those more general strategies, you’d expect some transfer to other domains.

But there’s still a gap between being good in an environment where you have a crisp reward and being good at something where success is ambiguous. If I ask for advice on a difficult decision, there isn’t a compiler that tells you whether your answer was correct. So I think verifiable tasks can be a very powerful engine for improving these models. How much of that improvement carries over to everything else is an empirical question. I’d want to measure it rather than assume it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says transfer from verifiable tasks to other domains is uncertain and should be measured rather than assumed, so gains need not extend to every task.
